title: Metaanalysis Model
text: I have been working on converting the Himmelstein (2022) advice-taking dual-hurdle model from a two-level cross-classified model, with responses cross-classified within judges and items, into a three-level cross-classified model, with responses cross-classified within judges and items and then nested within studies. To do this, I added a third level to the multilevel structure of the model that would account for study-level variance in the intercept estimates in both the part of the model that estimates the probabilities of Decline, Adopt, and Compromise (DAC) as well as the part that estimates the continuous Weight of Advice (WOA) values by modifying the Stan code and implementation in R. I then fit the model to the full dataset of WOA studies.

title: Metaanalysis Model
text:
Results
Displayed below is a plot of the distribution of WOA values as per the data and as per the model predictions. We can see the large proportion of WOA values near zero and one, with a range of values between as the DAC framework would expect.









One noticeable piece here is the bump at .5 exactly, with lower density surrounding it. This seems to be a study-level phenomenon—some studies have many responses with WOA values of exactly .5. Below are the studies with the highest proportions of the .5 responses.





The average proportion of .5’s in an given study was 5.24%.




It may be helpful to identify why certain studies have more responses of exactly .5 than others—the model seems to be fitting the data well across all values except the center.









Below we can see the distribution of the study-level intercepts for the probability of responses falling into the DAC categories. To the right we can see those box plots representing the distribution of those sampled intercepts for each study. We can see decent variability in these distributions between studies.









Next step is to decide how to handle these high .5 studies and to add predictors to the model! Looking forward to hearing what predictors would be best to include in this analysis. Also, if there are other ways of analyzing and presenting these results that would be helpful, please let me know!

title: Advice-Taking Metaanalysis
text:
This site is my log of work on converting the Himmelstein (2022) advice-taking dual-hurdle model to better model advice-taking in a metaanalytic context.




First, I converted the Himmelstein (2022) model from a two-level cross-classified model, with responses cross-classified within judges and items, into a three-level cross-classified model, with responses cross-classified within judges and items and then nested within studies.
One key initial finding from this metaanalysis is that some studies have a high proportion of Weight of Advice (WOA) values of exactly 0.5. To address this, we explored adding a third hurdle to the model.




Metaanalysis






With just one study that was high on 0.5s, we modified the original model to include an additional Midpoint hurdle.




Tri-Hurdle






With that model successfully estimated, we then merged the tri-hurdle and metaanalytic model frameworks.




Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis

Advice-Taking
Studies on advice taking often use a Judge Advisor System setup

○ Judge makes initial judgement


○ Judge receives advice


○ Judge makes final judgement

Outcome metric commonly “Weight of Advice” (WOA)




\[ WOA = \frac{\text{initial} - \text{final}}{\text{initial} - \text{advice}} \]






  
  
    \(WOA = 0\)
Decline
    \(WOA = 1\)
Adopt
    \(0 < WOA < 1\)
Compromise

Discrete

Decline, adopt, or compromise?
Categorical logit: estimates probability of each choice











Continuous

If compromise, how much?
Beta distribution: estimates continuous WOA between 0 and 1












(Himmelstein, 2022)

text:
Results
Displayed below is a plot of the distribution of WOA values as per the data and as per the model predictions. The model does seem to be overestimating the WOA = .5 values a bit. This is perhaps a prior issue (will see if we can fix).









Below is the same plot but broken up by study. The model does not seem to be overestimating the midpoint hurdle for every study, but it does for some. The studies with the most empirical responses around 0.5 seem like they might be the ones with the most overestimation.


Code
readRDS(here::here("Figures", "Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis", "ppc_plt_g.rds"))










Incorporating Predictors
Next, here are results from adding the predictors already in the dataset to the model! Here are the included predictors we have in this version:

Trial-Level: Distance, Confidence, Distance \(\times\) Confidence
Item-Level: None
Person-Level: Age, Gender, Confidence, Age \(\times\) Gender
Study-Level: Student Judge, Almanac Item, Future Item, Expert Advisor, Incentive

All these results are currently from a small version of the data (11 studies) for some preliminary results. For each predictor, we have a plot with levels of the predictor on the x-axis or in color. For the upper graphs on the plot, we have violin plots of the probabilities of the different discrete choices, and for the lower graph, we have the distribution of WOA values. The filled-in circle point is the mean WOA including the discrete choices, and the open circle point is the mean WOA not including decline or adopt (i.e., just compromise and midpoint).

Trial-Level


Code
saveRDS(woa_predictor_plt(playdat_full, c("distance", "confidence")),
        here::here("Figures", "Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis More Predictors", "distance-by-confidence_plt.rds"))




Code
readRDS(here::here("Figures", "Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis More Predictors", "distance-by-confidence_plt.rds"))





With increased distance, the probability of declining or adopting decreases, and the probability of adopting increases. With increased confidence, the probability of declining increases, and the probability of compromising decreases.






Person-Level


Code
saveRDS((woa_predictor_plt(playdat_full, c("age", "female"))) &
          scale_fill_manual("Gender",
                            values = c("-1 SD" = "#597993", "Mean" = "blue", "+1 SD" = "#e38693"),
                            labels = c("-1 SD" = "Male", "Mean" = "?", "+1 SD" = "Female")) &
          scale_color_manual("Gender",
                            values = c("-1 SD" = "#465F73", "Mean" = "blue", "+1 SD" = "#D95D6E"),
                            labels = c("-1 SD" = "Male", "Mean" = "?", "+1 SD" = "Female")),
        here::here("Figures", "Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis More Predictors", "age-by-female_plt.rds"))




Code
readRDS(here::here("Figures", "Tri-Hurdle Metaanalysis More Predictors", "age-by-female_plt.rds"))





Male participants tended to decline advice more, and this increased with age. Female participants were more likely to compromise, which increased with age, and male participants were less likely to compromise with age. Note: this effect seems like it lessened when I added in more data. Need varying slope?






Study-Level
Students declined advice less, compromised with advice less, and adopted advice more. When compromising, students tended to give more weight to the advice in their updated belief than did the non-students.
Studies with almanac items were more prone to perfect averaging.
Studies that had incentives showed lower rates of declining and adopting but higher rates of midpoint averaging and compromising. However, continuous compromises from these incentivized studies weighed their advice less in their updated judgement than did non-incentivized judgements.

Midpoint Hurdle Prior
Messing around with the prior specification for the standard deviation of the variance component of the cluster effects of the midpoint hurdle.
student_t_lpdf(sd_7 | 3, 0, 2.5) - 1 * student_t_lccdf(0 | 3, 0, 2.5)

Code
nu <- 3
mu <- 0
sigma <- 2.5

expand_grid(alpha = c(1), beta = c(10, 2, 1.5, 0.5)) |>
  pwalk(\(alpha, beta) {
    (data.frame(i = seq(0, 10, length.out = 1000)) |>
         mutate(dens_t = dt((i - mu) / sigma, df = nu) / sigma * 2,
                dens_g = dgamma(i, shape = alpha, scale = beta)) |>
         ggplot(aes(x = i, y = dens_t)) +
         geom_line() +
         geomtextpath::geom_textline(aes(y = dens_g,
                                         label = paste0("gamma(", alpha, 
                                                        ", ", beta, ")")),
                                     color = "skyblue3", size = 6) +
         coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, .5),
                         expand = F, clip = "off") +
         guides(y = "none") +
         labs(y = NULL, x= NULL) +
         theme_classic(base_size = 16)) |>
      print()})
